 🌊 HELLOBUSAN: The WebMCP Agent Governance Platform 

 
 💡 Core Question: "What if a city becomes machine-readable for AI agents, while humans retain absolute control?" 

 🚀 3 Key Breakthroughs: 

 
 🌐 WebMCP City OS: Replaces unstable DOM scraping with 10 explicit WebMCP Tool schemas. 
 🔐 Agent Wallet: Granular permission boundaries (Read: ALLOW / Book: ASK / Pay: DENY). 
 ⚡ Empirical Proof: 84% faster execution & 0% DOM parsing failures. 
 
 

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming capable of reasoning, planning, and taking actions on behalf of people. But most websites are still designed only for humans. 

 I asked a simple question: 

 What if a real city could become usable by AI agents, without taking control away from people? 

 This question led me to HELLOBUSAN. 

 I chose Busan as my real-world testbed because a single human goal can require many different services: discovering places, checking events, comparing restaurants, calculating routes, managing time, estimating costs, and eventually making reservations. 

 Normally, people have to move between many websites and applications to complete these tasks. 

 I wanted to explore a different model: 

 The human expresses the goal. 

 The Agent handles the complexity. 

 WebMCP connects the Agent to real web capabilities. 

 The human remains in control of consequential actions. 

 HELLOBUSAN is therefore not just another AI travel planner. 

 It is an experiment in designing a new relationship between Humans, Agents, and Cities. 

 What it does 

 HELLOBUSAN allows a person to describe what they want to accomplish in natural language. 

 For example: 

 
 “Plan a six-hour rainy-day trip in Busan for my family within a ₩50,000 budget.” 
 

 Instead of manually searching multiple services, the Agent can use WebMCP tools to discover information and coordinate actions. 

 The Agent can: 

 
 Search places, restaurants, and events 
 Retrieve detailed information 
 Check relevant conditions such as weather 
 Calculate routes and travel time 
 Estimate and optimize the budget 
 Build and update an itinerary 
 Coordinate multiple services around one user goal 
 

 The key difference is that HELLOBUSAN does not treat autonomy as unlimited permission. 

 I designed an Agent Permission Model: 
 Search ALLOW
Compare ALLOW
Route ALLOW
Schedule ALLOW
Reservation ASK
Payment DENY

 
 How I built it 

 HELLOBUSAN is designed as a WebMCP-based agentic interface with a Cloudflare-native backend. 

 Instead of requiring an Agent to interpret a website only through visual elements, HELLOBUSAN exposes structured capabilities through WebMCP tools. 

 My tool architecture includes capabilities such as: 

 
 search_places 
 search_restaurants 
 search_events 
 get_place_details 
 get_weather 
 calculate_route 
 estimate_cost 
 get_itinerary 
 update_itinerary 
 request_reservation 
 

 Each capability has a defined purpose and structured input/output schema. 

 I separated read operations, reversible actions, and consequential actions so that the Agent's level of autonomy can be controlled. 

 The application architecture uses: 

 
 React and TypeScript for the user interface 
 WebMCP for Agent-facing web capabilities 
 Cloudflare Workers for application logic and API routing 
 Cloudflare D1 for persistent application data 
 Cloudflare Durable Objects for stateful trip sessions and coordination 
 REST APIs and structured JSON data for service integration 
 

 A key design decision was to make permissions a system-level boundary rather than merely a visual setting. 

 The interface may show that payment is disabled, but the backend must also enforce that restriction. 

 I also designed an Agent Activity Log so that users can understand what the Agent is doing instead of experiencing an invisible autonomous process. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest challenge was not generating an itinerary. 

 It was deciding where autonomy should stop. 

 Giving an Agent more capabilities is technically attractive, but greater capability also creates greater responsibility. 

 I identified three different levels of action: 

 
 READ: The Agent can retrieve and understand information. 
 ACT: The Agent can perform reversible actions such as organizing an itinerary. 
 COMMIT: The Agent performs a consequential action that may affect the user. 
 

 The third category requires human approval. 

 This became particularly important when designing reservations and payments. 

 I deliberately avoided the assumption that: 

 
 “The user asked for a trip, therefore the Agent can do anything necessary to complete it.” 
 

 Instead, the system distinguishes between intent and authority. 

 A user's intention to “plan a trip” does not automatically grant permission to spend money or make an irreversible commitment. 

 Another challenge was making WebMCP meaningful rather than decorative. 

 I did not want to build a conventional travel application and simply add a WebMCP label. 

 The Agent interaction itself had to depend on structured capabilities. 

 I therefore designed the product around a comparison between conventional web interaction and WebMCP-based interaction, focusing on task steps, tool usage, errors, completion, and human approvals. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 My biggest accomplishment is that HELLOBUSAN turned WebMCP from a technical capability into a visible user experience. 

 The user does not need to understand WebMCP. 

 They simply express a goal. 

 Behind the interface, the Agent discovers available capabilities, calls structured tools, reasons over the results, updates the itinerary, and stops when human authorization is required. 

 I am especially proud of the Agent Wallet concept. 

 Instead of treating an Agent as either “fully autonomous” or “not autonomous,” I give the user granular control over what the Agent can do. 

 I am also proud of the Agent Activity / Black Box experience. 

 Users can see: 

 
 What the Agent is doing 
 Which tool it is using 
 What information it found 
 What it changed 
 Which permission it used 
 Where human approval is required 
 

 This makes autonomy visible. 

 Most importantly, the prototype demonstrates a different philosophy of agentic computing: 

 
 The goal is not to maximize what the Agent can do.

live_observation.first_impression: The page presents a human-controlled Busan trip-planning agent with a prefilled rainy-day family itinerary, map, budget slider, wallet permissions, and evaluation controls.
live_observation.action_attempted: Ran the visible "Run WebMCP Agent (Mode C)" control.
live_observation.after_state: The page remained visually and structurally unchanged; the evaluation table still showed dashes and no activity result appeared.
live_observation.notes: Permission boundaries were explicit: reservation required asking first, while payment and profile data were blocked.
